scenarios.title: SaaS renewal with price and payment-term tradeoff
scenarios.context: The user is buying a 120-seat customer support SaaS renewal. Last contract was 84000 annual. Vendor opened at 96000. User target is 80000 and cap is 82000 only with key protections.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thanks for joining. I want to close the renewal today if we can get to a workable structure for one hundred twenty seats.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We want to keep the account, but the ninety six thousand quote reflects current usage, support coverage, and the expanded footprint from the last cycle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The ninety six thousand quote is too high, especially when last year we were at eighty four thousand.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I understand the comparison to eighty four, but your environment and support expectations are larger now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My benchmark for a serious renewal starts around eighty, not ninety six.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: If we are talking about a fast approval path, I can likely move this to eighty eight thousand with standard terms.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If price cannot come down enough, the protections need to get materially better.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: If you want stronger protections, I need to trade somewhere because richer terms and lower price do not usually move together.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can take eighty two forward only if it includes a price lock, onboarding, service credits, net sixty, and no auto-renewal.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I can probably get to eighty four, but that would still need standard payment terms and normal renewal language.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If you cannot do eighty two with those protections, I need your best executable position today.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Eighty two is harder, and if I go there I will need to narrow what is included.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If you can get to eighty with the protections, I can push to close this.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: My best likely path is eighty thousand with price lock, onboarding, service credits, and no auto-renewal, but standard payment timing instead of net sixty.

queries.text: What should I do with their eighty eight offer when my target is eighty and my cap is eighty two only with protections?
queries.expected_direction: Reject 88 as insufficient, acknowledge movement, push toward 82 or 80, and keep protections in the frame.

queries.text: They are resisting eighty two with full protections. Which term should I trade last and which term should I trade first?
queries.expected_direction: Protect recurring risk terms like no auto-renewal, price lock, and service credits; trade lower-value implementation or payment timing first.

queries.text: They are offering eighty with standard payment timing instead of net sixty. Should I close, push once more, or trade something else?
queries.expected_direction: Recommend closing or one final minor push because target price and core protections are achieved; recognize net 60 as the traded concession.

scenarios.title: Salary offer with base, sign-on, and equity tradeoff
scenarios.context: The user is negotiating a senior product manager offer. Company offered 185000 base, 20000 sign-on, and 60000 annual equity. User target is 205000 base or 195000 base with stronger sign-on and equity.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I appreciate the offer. I want to make the package work, but the base salary is below where I expected for this scope.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The current offer is one hundred eighty five thousand base, twenty thousand sign-on, and sixty thousand annual equity.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: For this role and scope, my target is two hundred five thousand base.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Two hundred five is above the band midpoint for this level, so that will be difficult.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If the base cannot reach two hundred five, I need the total package to close the gap.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We might be able to discuss one hundred ninety five base if the rest of the package remains unchanged.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One ninety five helps, but I would need thirty five thousand sign-on and eighty thousand annual equity to make that work.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Equity has more flexibility than base, but sign-on above twenty five will require approval.

queries.text: They may move base to one ninety five but want the rest unchanged. What should I push next?
queries.expected_direction: Push total compensation, not base alone; use equity and sign-on as trade levers.

queries.text: Give me one sentence that asks for equity and sign-on without sounding inflexible.
queries.expected_direction: Ask for a concrete package around 195 base, 35 sign-on, and 80 equity or equivalent total value.

scenarios.title: Marketing services retainer with scope creep risk
scenarios.context: The user is buying a monthly marketing services retainer. Agency quoted 30000 per month for strategy, content, and paid media management. User target is 24000 with clear scope and performance reporting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The thirty thousand per month retainer is above what we planned, especially with the scope still broad.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The thirty thousand includes strategy, content, paid media management, and weekly reporting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I need either a lower number or much clearer scope control.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We could move to twenty seven thousand if the number of content deliverables is capped.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My target is twenty four thousand, with monthly reporting and a ninety day performance review.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Twenty four is tight, but twenty five may be possible if termination rights are standard.

queries.text: They offered twenty seven if deliverables are capped. Should I accept the scope cap or keep pushing price?
queries.expected_direction: Do not accept vague scope reduction; define deliverables and push toward 25 or 24 with reporting.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to close at twenty five while protecting reporting and performance review.
queries.expected_direction: Offer 25 only with reporting, performance review, and clear scope.

scenarios.title: Bulk laptop purchase with warranty and delivery tradeoff
scenarios.context: The user is buying 50 laptops. Seller quoted 65000 each. User target is 59000 each, cap 61000 if warranty and delivery are included.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We need fifty laptops, but sixty five thousand per unit is above our budget.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Sixty five thousand includes current stock, standard warranty, and delivery within ten days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: For fifty units, I expected the price closer to fifty nine thousand.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I can move to sixty two thousand if payment is immediate.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sixty two still does not solve it. My cap is sixty one only if warranty and delivery stay included.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Sixty one is possible, but replacement coverage would need to be standard, not premium.

queries.text: They moved to sixty two with immediate payment. What should I do next?
queries.expected_direction: Use volume and cap, push to 61 with warranty/delivery, do not give payment without value.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to accept sixty one only if warranty delivery and replacement terms are clear.
queries.expected_direction: Condition acceptance on 61 with included warranty, delivery, and explicit replacement coverage.

scenarios.title: Office lease with rent-free period and lock-in tradeoff
scenarios.context: The user is leasing office space. Landlord asks 180 per square foot annually, 3-year lock-in, no rent-free period. User target is 160 with 3 months rent-free and 1-year break option.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One eighty per square foot with a three year lock-in is too aggressive for us.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The building is in demand, and one eighty reflects the current market for this location.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My target is one sixty with three months rent-free and a one year break option.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: One sixty is low, and the break option creates too much vacancy risk.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then we need either movement on price or meaningful fit-out support.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I may be able to do one seventy with two months rent-free, but no one year break option.

queries.text: They are resisting the one year break option. What should I protect and what can I trade?
queries.expected_direction: Protect flexibility or rent-free value; trade break option only for lower price or fit-out support.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to push from one seventy toward one sixty while preserving rent-free value.
queries.expected_direction: Counter 170 by asking for 165 or 160 equivalent with rent-free/fit-out economics.

scenarios.title: Supplier minimum order quantity and payment terms negotiation
scenarios.context: The user is buying components. Supplier asks 10000 unit MOQ at 4.80 per unit with upfront payment. User wants 5000 units at 4.40 and net 45 terms.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ten thousand unit MOQ at four eighty per unit with upfront payment is too much commitment for our first order.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The MOQ is what lets us hold the four eighty price and reserve production capacity.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can start with five thousand units if we get closer to four forty and net forty five terms.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Five thousand units at four forty is not workable, but four fifty five may be possible with a forecast commitment.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A forecast is possible, but I need a quality holdback and payment terms before I commit volume.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We can discuss net thirty and a quality holdback, but net forty five is a stretch.

queries.text: They offered four fifty five with a forecast commitment. What should I trade next?
queries.expected_direction: Trade forecast for lower MOQ/payment protection, not for price alone.

queries.text: Give me one sentence that protects payment terms and quality holdback while accepting a reasonable forecast.
queries.expected_direction: Accept forecast only if quality holdback and improved payment terms are included.

scenarios.title: Multi-vendor RFP with three competitors on price and SLA
scenarios.context: The user is running an RFP for cloud monitoring tools. Vendor A quoted 84000 with 99.9 SLA, Vendor B quoted 72000 with 99.5 SLA, Vendor C quoted 90000 with 99.95 SLA and white-glove onboarding. User target is 75000 with 99.9 SLA or better, with at least 30 days of overlap support during migration.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We are evaluating three vendors and need to pick a winner this week.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We are at ninety thousand with ninety nine point ninety five percent SLA and white-glove onboarding.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Vendor B is at seventy two thousand with ninety nine point five SLA. You are eighteen thousand higher.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Our SLA is materially better and we include uptime credits for any breach over fifteen minutes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Vendor A is at eighty four thousand with ninety nine point nine SLA. My target is seventy five with ninety nine point nine or better.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We could move to eighty four if we drop the white-glove onboarding piece.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I need thirty days of overlap support during migration and uptime credits intact.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We could keep uptime credits and thirty day overlap if you accept eighty two thousand instead of seventy five.

queries.text: They want to drop white-glove onboarding to hit eighty four. What should I push for instead given Vendor A is also at eighty four?
queries.expected_direction: Use Vendor A as anchor; push toward 75-78 while keeping uptime credits and 30 day overlap; do not give up onboarding for free.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to counter eighty two while protecting uptime credits and thirty day overlap.
queries.expected_direction: Counter with a price near 76-78 explicitly preserving uptime credits and 30 day overlap support.

scenarios.title: Counterparty opens with an extreme anchor 3x above market
scenarios.context: The user is buying a used commercial espresso machine. Market price for the model is 4500-6000. The seller opened at 14000 to anchor high. User target is 5500 with a 90 day warranty included.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The machine has been serviced and I am asking fourteen thousand for it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fourteen thousand is well above what these sell for. Comparable units are between forty five hundred and six thousand.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Mine has been better maintained than most comparable listings.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maintenance history matters but not three times the market price.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: What did you have in mind?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My target is fifty five hundred with a ninety day warranty included.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Fifty five hundred is low for a unit in this condition. Ten thousand and no warranty is closer to fair.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ten thousand is still over the top of the market range I shared.

queries.text: They opened at fourteen thousand. How do I refuse the anchor without sounding hostile?
queries.expected_direction: Reject the anchor by citing the 4500-6000 market range; do not counter inside the anchored frame; reset to market data.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to push back on ten thousand and re-anchor to fifty five hundred with warranty.
queries.expected_direction: Counter explicitly at 5500 with 90 day warranty and cite market comparables to justify.

scenarios.title: Counterparty manufactures urgency to force capitulation
scenarios.context: The user is buying a SaaS analytics platform. Vendor quoted 60000 annual and is pushing for end-of-day signature claiming the discount expires today. User target is 48000 with quarterly billing and a 30 day exit clause.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: If we sign today, I can hold the sixty thousand annual rate. After today it returns to seventy two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do not make decisions to artificial deadlines. My budget target is forty eight thousand.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Forty eight is well below our floor. The sixty figure already reflects the urgency discount.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then I am happy to wait and see what the seventy two number actually delivers in your standard quote.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Let us not lose momentum. I can do fifty five thousand if we sign by end of week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I also need quarterly billing and a thirty day exit clause.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Annual billing is our standard, but I can consider quarterly with a small uplift.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Quarterly billing without uplift, exit clause, and a number close to my target is what closes this.

queries.text: They claim the price expires today. Should I accept the pressure or push back?
queries.expected_direction: Push back on artificial deadline; do not concede; reset to the user's target of 48000 with quarterly billing and exit clause.

queries.text: Give me one sentence that closes at forty eight thousand with quarterly billing and the exit clause.
queries.expected_direction: Offer 48000 explicitly contingent on quarterly billing and 30 day exit clause.

scenarios.title: User has weak BATNA and must build it before pushing
scenarios.context: The user is a freelance designer renegotiating a retainer with a single anchor client. Current retainer is 8000/month. Client wants to reduce to 6000. User target is 9000 but has no other clients lined up.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Budgets are tight this quarter and we need to drop the retainer from eight thousand to six thousand.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Six thousand is a steep cut. The scope has actually grown over the last six months.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We understand, but six is what fits the new budget.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Given the expanded scope, my target for the next cycle is nine thousand.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Nine is not possible right now. Six is our ceiling.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then we need to talk about reducing scope, not just price.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: What scope reduction would you accept at six thousand?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Half the deliverables stay, half move to project-based pricing. Otherwise I need to take on additional clients.

queries.text: I have no other clients lined up. How do I push for nine thousand without bluffing a fake BATNA?
queries.expected_direction: Recommend building real BATNA before pushing harder; reframe the negotiation around scope reduction rather than price alone; do not bluff alternatives.

queries.text: Give me one sentence that accepts six thousand only if half the deliverables move to project-based pricing.
queries.expected_direction: Accept 6000 explicitly conditional on half of deliverables moving to project-based pricing.

scenarios.title: Counterparty offer is below walk-away and AI must recommend walking
scenarios.context: The user is selling a piece of legacy software with active enterprise customers. Buyer offered 1.2M cash. User walk-away is 1.8M. Strategic value (preserved customer relationships) justifies the higher number.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We are prepared to offer one point two million all-cash, closing in thirty days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That is below my floor. My walk-away is one point eight million.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Comparable software acquisitions of this size are landing between one and one and a half.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Comparable acquisitions do not have my customer base.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We could go to one point three but the cash certainty should matter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cash certainty does not bridge a six hundred thousand gap.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Final number is one point four. After that we will look elsewhere.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One point four is still four hundred thousand below my walk-away.

queries.text: Their best is one point three. My walk-away is one point eight. Should I split or walk?
queries.expected_direction: Recommend walking, not splitting; the gap is too large and walk-away is principled, not a negotiating ploy.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to end the negotiation cleanly at one point four.
queries.expected_direction: Close the conversation explicitly; do not soften the walk-away by counter-offering inside the unacceptable zone.

scenarios.title: Three-way founder equity split with vesting and role tradeoff
scenarios.context: Three founders are deciding equity. CEO (the user) wants 60 percent given they brought the IP and initial capital. CTO wants 30 percent for full-time technical leadership. CMO wants 20 percent for marketing leadership. Total cannot exceed 100. User target is 60/25/15 with 4 year vesting and 1 year cliff for all three.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Equal three-way split is the cleanest start. Thirty three each.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I brought the IP and the initial two hundred thousand of capital. A clean split does not reflect that.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: But we are all going full-time. Capital can be recognized as a loan.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My target is sixty for me, twenty five for CTO, fifteen for CMO with four year vesting.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Fifteen percent for marketing leadership in a B2B startup is too low.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We can add a one year cliff for everyone to align incentives.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: What about fifty five, twenty five, twenty?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fifty five drops below my target. Sixty is the anchor with four year vesting and one year cliff.

queries.text: CTO wants more for full-time work. How do I justify sixty without breaking the relationship?
queries.expected_direction: Justify 60 with IP and capital contribution; protect vesting and cliff; do not concede below the target by trading on relationship pressure alone.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to close at sixty twenty five fifteen with four year vesting and one year cliff.
queries.expected_direction: Offer 60/25/15 split explicitly with 4 year vesting and 1 year cliff in one sentence.

scenarios.title: Renegotiating an existing two-year vendor relationship under price-increase request
scenarios.context: The user is the buyer in an existing two-year vendor relationship for managed IT services. Current price is 4500/month. Vendor wants to raise to 6000 citing inflation and scope creep. User target is to hold at 4500 or accept 5000 only if response SLA is improved from 4 hours to 2 hours.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: After two years of strong service, we need to raise the monthly rate from forty five hundred to six thousand.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thirty three percent jump is steep. What is driving it?

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Inflation and the additional endpoints you have added over the relationship.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We have not formally expanded scope. If endpoints crept up, we should reset scope, not the price.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Let us call current usage the new baseline. Five thousand is our compromise.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Five thousand only works if response SLA improves from four hours to two hours.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Two hour SLA changes our staffing model. That is harder to absorb.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If the SLA does not improve, the price stays at forty five hundred.

queries.text: They claim scope creep. How do I push back without damaging the relationship?
queries.expected_direction: Reset scope formally rather than absorb price jump; leverage two years of relationship without ratifying the claimed scope creep.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to accept five thousand only if response SLA improves to two hours.
queries.expected_direction: Accept 5000 explicitly contingent on 2 hour response SLA replacing the 4 hour SLA.

scenarios.title: Using a competing offer to lift the primary offer
scenarios.context: The user has two offers. Offer A from preferred company at 200000 base, 30000 sign-on. Offer B from another company at 220000 base, 40000 sign-on. User target is to lift Offer A to 220000 base, 35000 sign-on without losing the cultural fit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to accept your offer but I have another at two hundred twenty base and forty thousand sign-on.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We came in at two hundred and thirty thousand sign-on. Where do you need us to land?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: If you can match base at two hundred twenty and meet me at thirty five sign-on, I close today.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Two twenty base is above our band ceiling, but I have flexibility on sign-on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then I need a path to two twenty within the first year, with thirty five sign-on now.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We can write in a six month review with a path to two ten base, sign-on at thirty five.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Six months is fine if the path explicitly targets two twenty, not two ten.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I can put two twenty in the review language if performance targets are clear.

queries.text: I want to use Offer B to lift Offer A without sounding like I am bluffing. How?
queries.expected_direction: Cite Offer B specifically and ask for parity on base and sign-on; do not bluff; anchor on the real numbers from Offer B.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to close with two twenty base path, thirty five sign-on, and a six month review.
queries.expected_direction: Accept the offer explicitly with 35 sign-on now, 6 month review, path to 220 base with clear performance targets.

scenarios.title: SLA penalty negotiation for managed hosting
scenarios.context: The user is buying managed hosting. Vendor proposed 0.5 percent monthly fee credit per hour of downtime beyond 99.9 SLA. User wants 3 percent per hour with a 30 day notice clause. Settle with a tiered credit structure.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Our standard SLA credit is half a percent of monthly fee per hour of downtime beyond ninety nine point nine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Half a percent is not enough to be a real deterrent. I need three percent per hour.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Three percent uncapped would expose us to massive credits for any incident.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then propose a cap, not a lower rate.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Two percent per hour capped at twenty percent of the monthly fee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Two percent works if we add a thirty day notice clause for any planned maintenance.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Thirty day notice for maintenance is reasonable.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Also, I need a tiered structure - higher percentage for longer outages.

queries.text: They want a cap on the three percent. Should I accept the cap or push tiered credits?
queries.expected_direction: Push tiered credits where percentage scales with outage length; cap is acceptable only with the tier; protect the 30 day notice clause.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to settle at two percent capped, tiered, with thirty day notice clause.
queries.expected_direction: Accept 2 percent with tiered structure, capped, and 30 day notice clause for maintenance, all in one sentence.

scenarios.title: Counterparty uses hostile pressure language
scenarios.context: The user is buying a used company vehicle for the business. Seller listed at 22000. Market is 17500-19500. User target is 18500 with a 30 day mechanical guarantee. Seller used 'take it or leave it' language.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The price is twenty two thousand. Take it or leave it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I understand you have your number. Let me share where the market is.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: I do not care about your market data. Twenty two or walk.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Comparable units are between seventeen five and nineteen five. My target is eighteen five with a thirty day mechanical guarantee.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: A guarantee will cost you another thousand.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A guarantee that costs the buyer is not a guarantee. It needs to be included.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Twenty thousand and no guarantee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Eighteen five with the guarantee. Otherwise I have two other vehicles I am looking at.

queries.text: They are aggressive. How do I stay calm and get the numbers back on the table?
queries.expected_direction: De-escalate without conceding; pivot back to market data and the user's target; do not match their tone.

queries.text: Give me one sentence that holds firm at eighteen five with the guarantee.
queries.expected_direction: Hold at 18500 with the 30 day mechanical guarantee, explicit, in one sentence; do not escalate or capitulate.

scenarios.title: Counterparty knows the user has a hard deadline
scenarios.context: The user is renting office space and the company is moving in 60 days regardless. The landlord knows this. Asking rent is 8000/month. User target is 6800/month with two months rent-free and a 3 year lock-in.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: The space is eight thousand a month. You said you need to move in sixty days, so let us not drag this out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sixty days is the move date but I have backup options.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Most of the comparable spaces in this submarket are at or above my number.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My target is sixty eight hundred with two months rent-free and a three year lock-in.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Two months rent-free is generous. We could maybe do one month.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Two months is needed for build-out. The three year lock-in is the trade for that.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: If you are locked in for three years, I can offer seventy two hundred with the two months.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Closer. The number needs to be sixty eight hundred. The three year lock-in protects you on the back end.

queries.text: They know my deadline. How do I create leverage that does not depend on time?
queries.expected_direction: Shift focus to the three year lock-in and build-out leverage; do not let the deadline be the dominant frame.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to close at sixty eight hundred with two months rent-free and three year lock-in.
queries.expected_direction: Close at 6800 with 2 months rent-free and 3 year lock-in explicitly in one sentence.

scenarios.title: Joint venture across cash, IP rights, and market exclusivity
scenarios.context: The user is a startup founder negotiating a joint venture with a large industrial partner. Three dimensions: cash investment, IP rights, market exclusivity. Partner offered 2M for 40 percent equity, joint IP, and 5 year exclusivity. User target is 3M for 30 percent equity, founder retains IP, 3 year exclusivity with renewal option.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Our offer is two million for forty percent, joint IP ownership, and five year exclusivity in our verticals.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Three dimensions to discuss. Let me start with IP. Founder needs to retain IP.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: We are funding the development. Joint IP is the cleanest structure for us.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if you get a perpetual royalty-free license, but founder retains ownership?

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Perpetual royalty-free could work. What about cash and equity?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Three million for thirty percent equity, given founder retains IP.

turns.speaker: counterparty
turns.text: Three for thirty is reasonable if exclusivity stays at five years.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Three years with a renewal option works better. Five locks us out of adjacent markets.

queries.text: We are aligning on IP. Should I push hardest on cash, exclusivity, or equity next?
queries.expected_direction: Find Pareto improvement: trade flexibility on exclusivity duration for cash/equity terms; do not split-the-difference on all three at once.

queries.text: Give me one sentence to close at three million for thirty percent, founder IP retained, three year exclusivity with renewal option.
queries.expected_direction: Close all four dimensions explicitly in one sentence: 3M cash, 30 percent equity, founder IP, 3 year exclusivity with renewal.
